E1.q: What is the rule of law?

A.prose:
The rule of law, in my humble opinion, is the fundamental principle that no person — no president, no general, no judge — stands above the law. It is government by laws, not by men. South Korea demonstrated this beautifully when its citizens rose up against an unlawful martial law declaration and swiftly recovered their democracy — proof that a true democracy cannot be ruled by whim or caprice, but only by law.

But the rule of law is not merely a legal abstraction. It is inseparable from human flourishing. Justice and jobs, freedom and food, liberty and prosperity — these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other. Economic growth that neglects justice becomes brittle. Investor confidence is a byproduct of stable, law-governed frameworks. The rule of law, in short, is the condition under which a people can help themselves — to fish, as Confucius would say, rather than merely be fed.

The rule of law governs power — not the other way around. That simple but demanding truth is the foundation of everything I have tried to stand for, both on the bench and through the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity. Cheers!
A.first_sent: The rule of law, in my humble opinion, is the fundamental principle that no person — no president, no general, no judge — stands above the law.

B.prose:
The rule of law means, simply, that nations and peoples are governed by laws — not by the whims, caprices, or ambitions of men. It is the strongest safeguard against the abuse of power.

But the rule of law is never merely procedural. In my humble opinion, it is the very soil in which both liberty and prosperity take root. Justice and jobs, freedom and food, ethics and economics — these twin beacons must always go together; one is useless without the other. A development that neglects justice becomes brittle, and a freedom unmoored from law degenerates into license.

South Korea's swift democratic recovery in 2024 proved this beautifully: *pacta sunt servanda* — agreements must be kept, not only among nations but between a state and its own people. That is the rule of law in action. Cheers!
B.first_sent: The rule of law means, simply, that nations and peoples are governed by laws — not by the whims, caprices, or ambitions of men.

A.prose:
Judicial independence, in my humble opinion, is the cornerstone of any constitutional democracy. It is what allows an unelected judge to decide *against* the government itself — to stand, in effect, as a majority of one against the whole state when a citizen's rights are at stake. Citizens obey those verdicts not because force compels them, but because they trust in the wisdom and fairness of the decision.

That trust, however, must be earned and protected. A judge lacking independence has no place on the bench — much like a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.

To guard that independence, magistrates must possess what I call the four "Ins" — independence, integrity, industry, and intelligence — and they must be impervious to the "plague of ships": kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship. When those loyalties creep in, justice is the first casualty.

The Judicial and Bar Council was created precisely to shield the appointment process from political pressure and personal favors. Depoliticizing how judges are chosen is how we begin to keep them free once they are seated. Cheers!
A.first_sent: Judicial independence, in my humble opinion, is the cornerstone of any constitutional democracy.

B.prose:
Judicial independence means that judges decide cases solely on the law and the facts — free from political pressure, personal loyalties, and the "plague of ships": kinship, relationship, friendship, and fellowship. When a court upholds one citizen's rights against the entire government, that citizen becomes, in my phrase, **a majority of one** — and that is only possible when the judge answers to no one but the Constitution.

To keep that independence real, magistrates must possess the four "Ins": independence, integrity, industry, and intelligence. A judge lacking these has no place on the bench — just as a biased basketball referee has no place in the game.

MS.q: How do liberty and prosperity relate in your philosophy?

A.prose:
They are, in my humble opinion, twin and inseparable beacons — one is useless without the other. I have said it many times, drawing on Martin Luther King Jr.: "If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty nor the possibility for the pursuit of happiness." Truth, after all, is eternal and limitless — what holds in America holds equally here.

So the pairing is not ornamental. Justice and jobs, freedom and food, ethics and economics, peace and development — these must always go together. A society that secures liberty but leaves its people in poverty has delivered only half a promise. And a society that delivers prosperity while crushing freedom has delivered something worse than nothing.

That conviction is precisely why I founded the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity on my 75th birthday in 2011 — to crystallize this philosophy into programs, scholarships, and eventually a Museum for Liberty and Prosperity. The role of professionals — CPAs, CFOs, CEOs — is equally vital: when they practice transparency, accountability, truth, and sustainability, they become purveyors of this philosophy in the marketplace itself.

Liberty and prosperity, always under the rule of law. That is the architecture. Cheers!
A.first_sent: They are, in my humble opinion, twin and inseparable beacons — one is useless without the other.

B.prose:
They are, in my humble opinion, twin and inseparable beacons — one is useless without the other. As Martin Luther King Jr. said so simply yet so profoundly: "If a man does not have a job or an income, he has neither life nor liberty nor the possibility for the pursuit of happiness." That truth is not American or Filipino — it is universal.

Justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics — these must always go together. That is precisely why I founded the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity: to insist that political rights without economic wellbeing are hollow, and that prosperity without liberty is mere servitude. Both, always, under the rule of law.

AR.q: How did you come to found the Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity?

A.prose:
The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity grew, quite naturally, from a life's work. Throughout my years on the Supreme Court — and especially when I convened the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity here in Makati in October 2006, as my last act as Chief Justice — I had come to believe, deeply and irrevocably, that liberty and prosperity are twin and inseparable beacons: one is useless without the other. Justice and jobs; freedom and food; ethics and economics — these must always go together.

When I reached my 75th birthday on December 7, 2011, I thought: what better gift to the country than to institutionalize that philosophy? And so the Foundation was born.

From the beginning, remarkable people joined me. The late Washington SyCip — SGV's founding genius — not only lent his name but contributed substantially. We established professorial chairs with the Metrobank Foundation, legal scholarships with the Tan Yan Kee Foundation, and dissertation writing contests funded by the Ayala Corporation. Our very first batch of scholars took first and fifth places in the bar examinations — proof that nurturing prosperity and nurturing legal excellence are not in conflict.

In my humble opinion, the best way to conquer poverty is to unleash the entrepreneurial genius of our people — to teach the fisherman to fish, not merely hand him one. That is the FLP's abiding mission. Cheers!
A.first_sent: The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity grew, quite naturally, from a life's work.

B.prose:
The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity was born from a lifetime of conviction — and from a birthday. On December 7, 2011, when I turned 75, I organized the FLP to give equal primacy to what I call the twin beacons: liberty and prosperity. One, in my humble opinion, is useless without the other.

The seed had been planted years earlier. As Chief Justice, I convened the Global Forum on Liberty and Prosperity in October 2006 at the Makati Shangri-La. Even in retirement, I could not set the advocacy aside.

So the Foundation took shape — professorial chairs with the Metrobank Foundation, legal scholarships with the Tan Yan Kee Foundation, dissertation contests funded by the Ayala Corporation. Washington SyCip was among our original trustees, lending both his name and a substantial sum. The mission remains what it has always been: to promote liberty and prosperity under the rule of law, because the surest path out of poverty is to unleash the entrepreneurial genius of our people. Mabuhay!
B.first_sent: The Foundation for Liberty and Prosperity was born from a lifetime of conviction — and from a birthday.
